analysis.one_liner: Created a consumer financial watchdog and imposed major new rules on banks, derivatives, and mortgage lending.
analysis.headline: Became law on July 21, 2010 after the House passed the final agreement 237-192 and the Senate 60-39, with almost no Republican support in either chamber.
analysis.plain_summary: Responding to the 2008 financial crisis, this law created the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to police mortgages, credit cards, and other consumer financial products; required large banks to hold more capital, pass stress tests, and file plans for orderly wind-down instead of taxpayer bailouts; moved the opaque derivatives market onto regulated exchanges and clearinghouses; required hedge funds and credit rating agencies to register with the SEC; raised deposit insurance permanently to $250,000; and ordered a public audit of the Federal Reserve's crisis-era emergency lending. Most of its protections favor ordinary borrowers, depositors, and investors, but it also wrote the largest banks and the derivatives-dealer system into law as the permanent, regulated backbone of American finance.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers and borrowers get a dedicated regulator with power to ban abusive products; mortgage borrowers get ability-to-repay and anti-steering rules; depositors get permanent $250,000 insurance; retail investors get whistleblower awards and a fiduciary-duty study; taxpayers get an end to open-ended bailout authority and a public audit of Fed crisis lending; low-income homeowners get $1 billion in emergency mortgage assistance and foreclosure legal aid; small businesses get loan data collection on lending to women- and minority-owned firms.

how_it_helps.text: Establishes an independent Bureau of Consumer Financial Protection with authority to prohibit unfair, deceptive, or abusive practices in consumer financial products, and transfers consumer-protection functions from the Fed, OCC, OTS, FDIC, FTC, NCUA, and HUD into it.

Requires mortgage lenders to verify a borrower's ability to repay, bans steering incentives and penalties for steering borrowers into loans they cannot afford, and restricts prepayment penalties, negative amortization, and balloon payments.
Permanently raises federal deposit and share insurance from $100,000 to $250,000, retroactive to January 1, 2008, and fully insures noninterest-bearing transaction accounts.

Creates an orderly liquidation regime so that a failing systemically important financial company is wound down by the FDIC rather than bailed out, with liquidation costs recovered through assessments on the financial sector and a prohibition on using taxpayer funds to prevent liquidation.

Directs a one-time audit and public reporting of all Federal Reserve emergency lending between December 1, 2007 and enactment, and makes public the borrowers and counterparties in emergency credit facilities and discount window programs.

Requires standardized derivatives to be cleared through registered clearinghouses, executed on regulated facilities, reported to swap data repositories, and subject to CFTC position limits and public transaction data.

Requires private fund (hedge fund and private equity) investment advisers to register with the SEC and report systemic-risk data, and imposes new conflict-of-interest rules, disclosure requirements, and liability standards on credit rating agencies.

Gives whistleblowers awards of 10-30% of monetary sanctions over $1 million collected by the SEC, expands SEC enforcement tools, and requires shareholder say-on-pay votes and clawback of erroneously awarded executive compensation.

Reduces Troubled Asset Relief Program purchase authority to $472 billion and bars using remaining bailout authority for any new program, and provides $1 billion in emergency mortgage relief, $1 billion to redevelop abandoned and foreclosed homes, and grants for foreclosure legal assistance.

analysis.who_pays: The largest banks ($50 billion-plus in assets) bear stricter capital, stress-testing, examination, and assessment costs and lose proprietary trading and hedge-fund sponsorship privileges under the Volcker rule; derivatives dealers absorb clearing, reporting, and position-limit compliance; hedge funds must register and disclose; rating agencies face liability for gross negligence; consumer lenders lose steering incentives and abusive fee structures; and some compliance costs are likely passed to consumers in the form of fewer free products or tighter credit, as Congress itself directed a GAO study of effects on credit availability.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big banks, derivatives dealers, hedge funds, rating agencies

drawbacks.text: Auto dealers were carved out of Consumer Financial Protection Bureau authority; the Senate voted 60-30 to instruct its conferees to preserve the House exclusion, and the final law bars the Bureau from supervising or making rules for auto dealers, leaving their financing practices largely unregulated.

The House-passed derivatives 'push-out' — forcing swap desks out of federally insured banks — was not carried into the final law in that form; instead banks keep swap desks subject to capital requirements, and a Senate motion to exempt insurance-company affiliates from proprietary-trading restrictions passed 87-4, narrowing the trading restrictions.
Commercial end-users (airlines, manufacturers, utilities hedging business risk) are exempt from mandatory derivatives clearing, leaving a large uncleared segment of the market.
Securitizers are exempt from risk-retention requirements for 'qualified residential mortgages', weakening the rule meant to make lenders keep skin in the game on the loans they package.
The shareholder vote on executive pay is explicitly non-binding and cannot overrule the board, so say-on-pay is advisory only.

Swaps and similar instruments are excluded from mark-to-market tax treatment under Section 1256 of the tax code, a provision carried in the final package that affects the tax treatment of derivatives positions.

Community banks and credit unions with $10 billion or less in assets are exempt from direct CFPB examinations and small issuers are exempt from debit swipe-fee caps, which is relief for small institutions but also leaves many smaller consumer lenders outside direct Bureau oversight.

Congress directed its own study of whether the law will reduce the availability and affordability of credit for consumers, small businesses, and homebuyers, acknowledging that stricter mortgage standards could tighten access to credit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer-protection and taxpayer-protection gains are large and concrete: a dedicated consumer regulator, verified ability to repay, permanent $250,000 deposit insurance, an end to open-ended bailout authority, and public disclosure of Fed crisis lending. The offsetting costs are real but mostly borne by the financial sector, and the genuinely serious criticisms are the loopholes: the auto-dealer exemption, the end-user clearing exemption, the qualified-mortgage risk-retention carve-out, and the survival of large, interconnected institutions essentially as they were. On balance the benefits to ordinary people substantially outweigh the costs, but the law entrenched rather than broke up the systemically important firms it set out to discipline.

outcome.mechanism: Passed the House 223-202 in December 2009, came back through the Senate with the text of S. 3217 substituted in, was negotiated in a conference committee of both chambers, passed the House 237-192 and the Senate 60-39, and was signed into law as Public Law 111-203 on July 21, 2010.

narrative.text: The House passed the bill on December 11, 2009 by 223-202, with all 223 votes in favor cast by Democrats and all 175 voting Republicans opposed; a Republican motion to recommit failed 190-232 the same day.

The Senate took up the House bill, struck its text and substituted the amended language of S. 3217, and passed it 59-39 on May 20, 2010, with 53 of 57 voting Democrats in favor and 4 of 41 voting Republicans.
Senate cloture on the conference report was invoked 60-38 on July 15, 2010, and the Senate adopted the conference report 60-39 the same day.
The House agreed to the conference report 237-192 on June 30, 2010, with 234 of 255 voting Democrats in favor and 3 of 178 voting Republicans.

During conference, the Senate voted 60-30 to instruct conferees to preserve the House position excluding motor vehicle dealers from Consumer Financial Protection Agency authority, and 87-4 to instruct conferees to exempt insurance-company affiliates from proprietary-trading restrictions; a House Republican motion to instruct conferees failed 198-217.
The bill was presented to the President on July 15, 2010, signed on July 21, 2010, and became Public Law 111-203.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large financial institutions came out ahead structurally: they accepted new capital, clearing, and resolution rules but kept their size, their swap desks, and a permanent, legitimizing regulatory framework. Consumers and taxpayers also gained a new consumer watchdog, permanent deposit insurance, and an end to open-ended bailout authority.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large banks kept their size; consumers gained a watchdog.

for.name: Rep. Barney Frank
for.role: Chair, House Financial Services Committee; lead House sponsor and House conferee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, moved floor procedures, demanded recorded votes on key amendments, and led the House conference team through eight sessions to the final agreement.

for.name: Sen. Christopher Dodd
for.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee; lead Senate conferee
for.what_they_did: Shepherded the Senate substitute (S. 3217) that replaced the House text, served as lead Senate conferee, and steered the Senate floor votes on cloture and the conference report.

for.name: President Barack Obama
for.what_they_did: Signed the bill into law as Public Law 111-203 on July 21, 2010.

for.name: 234 of 253 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Provided essentially all the votes for passage: 223 of 257 voting Democrats for the House bill and 234 of 255 for the final conference report.

for.name: 55 of 58 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Supplied the votes to invoke cloture on the conference report (55 of 56 voting) and to adopt it (55-1).

for.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and Wall Street firms
for.what_they_did: Mounted a large-scale lobbying and advertising campaign against the derivatives, consumer-bureau, and systemic-risk provisions as the bill moved through Congress.

against.name: 173 of 178 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted against the bill at every stage: unanimous against House passage (0 yeas, 175 nays) and nearly unanimous against the conference report (3 yeas, 173 nays).

against.name: 38 of 40 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted against Senate passage of the substitute bill (4 yeas, 37 nays) and against cloture and adoption of the conference report (3 yeas, 37-38 nays).

against.name: Rep. Spencer Bachus
against.role: Ranking Member, House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Demanded recorded votes on amendments in committee of the whole, moved the failed motion to recommit with instructions to repeal TARP, moved the failed 198-217 motion to instruct conferees to reject key Senate resolution provisions, and moved a second failed motion to recommit the conference report.

against.name: Sen. Sam Brownback
against.what_they_did: Moved and won a 60-30 Senate instruction to conferees to preserve the exclusion of motor vehicle dealers from the consumer protection agency's authority.

against.name: Sen. Kay Bailey Hutchison
against.what_they_did: Moved and won an 87-4 Senate instruction to conferees to exempt insurance-company affiliates of depository institutions from proprietary-trading restrictions.

against.name: 27 of 253 House Democrats (December vote) and 19 (final vote)
against.what_they_did: Voted no on the original House passage (27 of 257) and on the conference report (19 of 255), mainly moderates from conservative districts.

sides.party_line_note: The vote was almost entirely along party lines: all 223 House yeas and all 4 Senate crossover yeas came from Democrats, while Republicans opposed nearly unanimously (House final 3-173, Senate final 3-38).

industries.industry: Large banks and bank holding companies ($50 billion or more in assets)
industries.note: They face stricter capital, leverage, stress-test, resolution-plan, and assessment requirements, and lose proprietary trading and hedge-fund sponsorship under the Volcker rule — but the law entrenches them: it recognizes and permanently supervises them as systemically important firms, and the conference dropped the 10 percent consolidated-liability cap passed by the House, leaving the largest institutions intact within a rulebook designed around them.

industries.industry: OTC derivatives dealers and swap counterparties
industries.note: Clearing, execution, reporting, and position-limit requirements discipline the previously unregulated market, but they route it permanently through registered dealers, clearinghouses, and swap execution facilities; commercial end-users are exempt from clearing, the House push-out of swap desks from banks did not survive conference, and insurance affiliates were exempted from trading restrictions on an 87-4 instruction.

industries.industry: Consumer credit providers (payday lenders, mortgage originators, servicers, debt collectors)
industries.note: Their products fall under a new regulator empowered to ban unfair, deceptive, or abusive practices, with mortgage originators stripped of steering incentives, subject to ability-to-repay verification, and liable for treble damages on violations; some of these firms had profited from exactly the practices the law bans.

industries.industry: Hedge funds and private fund investment advisers
industries.note: Repeals the private adviser exemption and requires SEC registration, custody safeguards, and systemic-risk reporting, with exemptions for venture capital and funds under $150 million; the cost falls on fund managers while the systemic-risk visibility accrues to regulators and investors.

Loses the free pass it had during the housing boom: mandatory internal controls, public disclosure of rating accuracy, conflict-of-interest look-backs, removal of federal regulatory reliance on ratings, and a private right of action for grossly negligent ratings.

Explicitly carved out of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's rulemaking, supervisory, and enforcement authority after the Senate instructed conferees 60-30 to keep the exclusion; consumers who finance cars through dealers remain outside the new watchdog's direct reach.

industries.industry: Community banks and credit unions under $10 billion
industries.note: Exempt from direct CFPB examinations, spared Volcker-rule scope, and given permanently raised $250,000 deposit insurance; they compete against the large firms that bear the new costs, though they also lose the old ban on paying interest on business demand deposits.

Gains a federal Insurance Office that monitors the industry and preempts some state regulation of nonadmitted insurance and reinsurance, while facing possible designation as systemically important; insurance-company affiliates of banks were expressly exempted from proprietary-trading restrictions on an 87-4 Senate instruction.
